opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ethan, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yo, yeah, let's do it. I edit videos for clients and I make my own stuff online too. AI's all over my work already, so I've got thoughts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are honestly sick. I can do in an hour what used to take a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The catch is the clients know that too. So they pay me like it took an hour. I'm doing more work for about the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take on more clients to make up for the lower rates, and post more of my own videos to grow my channel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of uneasy. Excited about the tools, annoyed about the money.

S0.say: The tools are honestly sick. I can do in an hour what used to take a day.
S0.think: Clients know that too, so they pay me like it took an hour. More work for about the same money.
S0.do: Takes on more clients to make up for lower rates and posts more of his own videos.
S0.feel: Excited about the tools, annoyed about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies not hiring beginners is wild. Like, where do people learn?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm freelance, so nobody was hiring me anyway. But small businesses that used to pay me for a simple promo will just make it themselves with an app. The easy jobs go first, and the easy jobs are most of my jobs right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to niche down. Maybe music videos or weddings, stuff where people want a real person with taste. And I'd actually set up a proper rate card instead of winging it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Kind of a slow squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd 'actually' do the rate card. Is that a habit, winging it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, guilty. I'm better at the creative stuff than the business stuff. This would force me to fix that.

S1.say: Companies not hiring beginners is wild. Where do people learn?
S1.think: Small businesses will make simple promos with an app. The easy jobs go first, and they're most of my work right now.
S1.do: Niches into music videos or weddings where taste matters, and finally sets up a proper rate card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post about how the big AI companies trained their tools on creators' work without paying us, and now they're selling it back to our clients. That's messed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office layoffs mean businesses cut marketing budgets, and the first thing cut is the freelancer. Some new AI jobs might suit me, like prompting video tools for agencies. But I'd be up against every other editor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch myself to agencies as the person who knows the AI video tools best. And I'd stop spending on gear, keep living with my parents and try to pay them a bit of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like every month could be the bad one.

S2.say: Big AI companies trained their tools on creators' work without paying us, and now sell it back to our clients.
S2.think: Layoffs mean marketing cuts, and freelancers go first. The new AI jobs might suit me, but every other editor wants them too.
S2.do: Pitches himself to agencies as an AI video expert, stops buying gear and stays with his parents, paying a little rent.
S2.feel: Like every month could be the bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tax the AI companies and give everyone a basic income. Artists and creators especially got robbed here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches skilled pros, it matches skilled editors. Paid client work would mostly dry up. My own channel is the only thing I'd have, and that's tiny. I'd be living at my parents' place with no real income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on my channel for a few months, try every platform, and get a part-time job somewhere physical, like a café or a warehouse, since that's safe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the thing I'm good at stopped being worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go 'all in' on your channel and also get a part-time job. Which comes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job, if I'm being real. My parents would make me. The channel is evenings.

S3.say: Tax the AI companies and give everyone a basic income. Creators especially got robbed.
S3.think: Paid editing would mostly dry up. My own channel is all I'd have, and it's tiny.
S3.do: Gets a part-time café or warehouse job first, and grows his channel in the evenings across every platform.
S3.feel: Like what he's good at stopped being worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the whole economy is being handed to a few companies. Everyone should be in the streets about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in cafés and warehouses take my backup job. So I'd have nothing paid at all. Weird thing is, if everyone's out of work, maybe more people watch videos. But views aren't money unless someone's buying ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at my parents' and try to keep making content, maybe teach people how to use the AI tools in videos, since everyone would be trying to learn. And sign up for any support going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Still kind of hoping something clicks, though.

S4.say: The whole economy is being handed to a few companies. Everyone should be in the streets.
S4.think: Robots take my café or warehouse backup, so I'd have no paid work. More people might watch videos, but views aren't money.
S4.do: Stays at his parents', makes videos teaching AI tools and signs up for any support available.
